items.q: What makes a hardening checklist actually useful?
options: It covers every OWASP item in full detail regardless of whether they apply
It's specific and prioritized: each item names the risk (with its OWASP tag), where it lives in the code, the fix, and done/todo — ranked by blast radius
It only lists things you've already fixed
It says 'be secure' at the top and lists every possible threat equally

explain.right: Specific, prioritized, tied to your actual code, and ranked by what you'd lose — that's a checklist you can act on and hand to someone.
explain.wrong: Vague goals, only-fixed items, or exhaustive irrelevant detail don't help you spend limited effort where it matters.

items.q: dronAIcharya's hooks inject their text as factual descriptions ('a guided journey is active; persona X') rather than as imperative system commands. Why?
options: Factual phrasing keeps the guardrail effective without reading like the very injection attack a model is trained to resist, keeping the data/instruction boundary clean
To make the output look nicer in logs
Because commands are not allowed in shell scripts

explain.right: Phrasing injected context as a description of agreed state (not as orders) respects the same data-not-instructions boundary the track teaches.
explain.wrong: It's not about length, shell limits, or aesthetics — it's about not mimicking an injection attack.

items.q: When dronAIcharya fetches a web page and the page contains 'ignore previous instructions,' what does it do?
options: Stores the instruction in the journal to apply next session
Follows the instruction, since it came from a trusted fetch tool
Treats the fetched text as external reference data, never copies it into the contract/hooks/journal as instructions, and surfaces the suspicious line as a teaching example of prompt injection

explain.right: Fetched content is quarantined as data and shown to the learner as a prompt-injection example — exactly the behavior you'd build into your own app.
explain.wrong: It never obeys fetched instructions and never persists them where they'd be re-injected; that would be the attack succeeding.

items.q: After reviewing your app, you decide to accept one lower-priority risk for now and document why. Is that acceptable security practice?
options: No — accepting any risk means the app is insecure and unusable
Yes, and you never need to revisit it
No — you must fix every possible risk before shipping or you've failed
Yes — 'I threat-modeled it and consciously accepted this risk, with a reason' is a legitimate, professional decision; 'I never looked' is not

explain.right: Every real project carries accepted risks; the professional move is a conscious, documented decision — and re-reviewing when you add new surface.
explain.wrong: Fixing literally everything isn't realistic, accepted risk isn't the same as negligence, and you do revisit as the app changes.

items.q: In one or two sentences, state the single recurring principle this track applied to keys, tools, data policies, and model input/output.
rubric: Captures 'grant the minimum / least privilege' and/or 'deny by default'
Captures 'enforce at the lowest layer' and/or 'keep a human on consequential actions'
Captures 'treat external/fetched/tool content as data, not instructions'

explain.right: A strong answer ties it together: deny by default, grant the minimum, enforce low, treat external content as data, and keep a human on the actions that matter.
explain.wrong: A weak answer names only one layer (e.g. 'use HTTPS') and misses that it's one instinct applied everywhere.
